name: theworldofai.org AI Laws: US state AI bill tracker and comparison
title: theworldofai.org AI Laws: US state AI bill tracker and comparison
answer: This is the AI Laws section of theworldofai.org, a free reference site that tracks United States artificial intelligence legislation. It reports 6,003 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to each bill's official page. Its most useful content is a comparison of 103 enacted measures across 27 states, reviewed on 18 September 2026, which found that no two states wrote the same law but that recurring duties do exist, including telling people when they deal with AI and keeping a qualified person in decisions about health, employment, benefits or education.

sections.body: The AI Laws section is published by theworldofai.org, a site that describes itself as an atlas of artificial intelligence covering what the law says, who is suing whom and what the words mean. It is a free to read, free to cite reference page, rebuilt daily from primary sources, and it carries the date each page was last verified. Its scope is United States state artificial intelligence legislation, drawn from the LegiScan legislative database, with each bill linked to its official page. The comparison of enacted measures was reviewed on 18 September 2026. The page also promotes books and consulting services by Stephen R. Jordan, including a novel, The AI Lawyer, published on 17 August 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page tracks 6,003 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to each bill's official page. Its substance is a comparison of 103 enacted measures across 27 states, reviewed on 18 September 2026. It reports that only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149, while every other measure names a single setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where the stakes are personal, the same rule recurs: AI may assist but may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. Attorneys general enforce the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states treat a violation as an unfair or deceptive trade practice. Insurance commissioners, licensing boards and election agencies handle their own sectors. A private right to sue is the exception.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states 6,003 AI bills tracked across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan. It states that 103 enacted measures across 27 states were compared, reviewed on 18 September 2026. It states that only Colorado, in CO SB189, and Texas, in TX HB149, passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors. It states that no state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law, that attorneys general enforce the larger laws often exclusively, and that a private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Government gets a live index of state bills plus a summary of what has actually been enacted. The most directly relevant point is that New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions, which sits alongside the recurring pattern that AI may assist but not be the only decider in health, employment, benefits or education. The source also matters for enforcement: it says no state created a new agency, so attorneys general are the enforcers a public body or supplier is most likely to meet, and several states treat violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: This is a tracker and a summary, not legal advice, and it covers state legislation only. The harvested text does not describe a federal register watch, so that part of the industry page is not supported here. It gives no bill text, only links, and its figures are a snapshot from the harvest date. The page is partly commercial, promoting books, audits and consulting services by Stephen R. Jordan, and it offers no independent verification of the patterns it reports.
